# Hot Brakes, Wheel Sticks

A brake system that generates excessive heat on one side while the opposite wheel spins freely indicates a mechanical imbalance rather than a simple component failure. In your specific case, replacing both rotors and pads recently only to see the same symptoms return suggests you are fighting against an underlying installation or geometry issue. The fact that the left wheel requires significant force to rotate by hand on a jack is the primary diagnostic clue; it confirms internal drag within the caliper assembly.

This drag creates friction that converts kinetic energy into thermal energy. If the caliper piston is not seating fully, if the slide pins are binding, or if there is debris wedged in the brake pad clips, the pads will remain in contact with the rotor even when the pedal is released. Over time, this constant light friction generates enough heat to smoke old components and warp new ones. Since you replaced the hardware but the problem persisted, the issue likely lies in how that hardware was mounted or the alignment of the suspension components supporting it.

### Caliper Slide Pin Maintenance

The most common cause for one-sided sticking is seized caliper slide pins. These small bolts allow the floating caliper to move laterally as the pads wear. If these pins are not cleaned, lubricated with high-temperature grease, and torqued correctly during reassembly, they will seize. Once seized, the caliper cannot retract fully after braking.

When you replaced the ball joints last fall, it is highly probable that the slide pin bolts were disturbed or not properly addressed. If you reused old pins without inspecting them for corrosion or simply applied general-purpose grease instead of a dedicated brake caliper grease, the friction coefficient increases significantly. This prevents the caliper from sliding smoothly, causing the rotor to rub against the pad even when stationary. The heat buildup you experienced previously likely accelerated this binding process, making it worse with every stop-and-go cycle.

### Suspension Geometry and Toe In

You asked whether an alignment issue could cause brakes to stick on one side. While toe settings primarily affect tire wear and vehicle tracking, they can indirectly influence brake drag through suspension geometry changes. However, the direct correlation is usually less about "toe" and more about how the ball joint replacement affected the caliper's mounting plane.

If the ball joints were replaced without restoring the original suspension geometry precisely, the control arm may be sitting at a slightly different angle. This can alter the orientation of the brake caliper bracket relative to the rotor. Even a minor deviation in the mount point can cause the pads to sit unevenly against the rotor surface, creating a "high spot" that generates drag. Additionally, if the ball joint bushings were not perfectly aligned during installation, the caliper may be pulled slightly off-center, preventing full retraction of the piston.

### Diagnostic Steps and Verification

Before condemning the entire assembly or replacing expensive parts again, perform a specific isolation test. With the vehicle safely lifted and secured on jack stands:

1.  Remove the wheel and inspect the slide pins visually for rust or lack of grease.
2.  Manually push the caliper piston back using C-clamps (with the brake lines disconnected) to ensure the cylinder seals are functioning correctly.
3.  Rotate the rotor by hand. If it still feels tight, apply a penetrating fluid specifically designed for rusted hardware to the slide pin boots and gently wiggle the caliper back and forth.
4.  Check the ball joint play. Excessive lateral movement in the lower control arm can cause the caliper bracket to shift position under load, leading to intermittent drag that manifests as heat.

It is also worth noting that a crimped line replacement mentioned in your history suggests previous corrosion issues. If the new line was not bled correctly or if air remains trapped near the wheel cylinder, it could mimic a sticking brake feel, though this usually presents as a spongy pedal rather than extreme rotor heat.

### Preventive Measures for Future Replacements

To prevent recurrence, adhere to strict torque specifications when reinstalling caliper brackets and slide pins. Use a thread locker appropriate for high-heat applications if the manufacturer recommends it, but ensure you do not overtighten the slide pin bolts, as this can distort the caliper body and cause uneven pad contact. Always install new rubber boots on the slide pins to protect against moisture intrusion, which is the leading cause of seizure over time.

If the ball joint replacement was performed by a third party, verify that the suspension was aligned afterward. An alignment ensures that the control arms are parallel to their intended design angles, minimizing any lateral stress on the brake assembly that could lead to rubbing or heat generation. Addressing these mechanical nuances now will save you from warping new rotors again and ensure consistent braking performance without the distraction of overheating components.
